To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic low-dose-rate irradiation of Japanese medaka at 350 mGy d-1 resulted in a decrease in the percentage of hatchlings and a decrease in the number of eggs per day produced.
chronic low-level exposures of Japanese medaka to ionizing radiation resulted in fewer eggs per day, lower percentages of viable eggs, and lower percentages of hatchlings.

chronic low-level irradiations at the 10 mSv y(-1) dose level (the current international guideline for radiation protection of aquatic biotas) can cause significant reductions in the number of eggs produced per day and the percentage of hatchlings, but not in the number of hatchlings produced per day, for the model organism, medaka.

the effects of chronic exposures to low-level ionizing radiation.
the effects of low dose rate irradiation at the population level.

the effects of chronic exposures to radiation at levels below those associated with deterministic effects, but above background radiation levels, and the LoDIF is an appropriate tool for conducting such studies.

the LoDIF is a unique facility that is designed for research on chronic exposures to low-level irradiation, and that the pilot study demonstrates the utility of this facility and the Japanese medaka for such research.
chronic exposures to low dose rates of radiation have the potential to cause significant effects in the population of medaka.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have successfully constructed and commissioned a unique facility that will allow us to test the effects of chronic exposures to radiation on a variety of aquatic organisms.
chronic low-level irradiations of 350 mGy d-1 are likely to have population-level impacts, and therefore should not be considered safe for aquatic biota.
